items.title: PUCT Project 58000, rulemaking to update ERCOT transmission cost recovery, comment deadline reached
items.summary: The Public Utility Commission of Texas is amending its wholesale and investor owned utility retail transmission cost recovery rules for the ERCOT region. The commission published a proposal for publication amending Section 25.192 and Section 25.193 and adding a new Section 25.252, and set a comment deadline of August 11th, 2026. Utilities and data center developers filed comments on the deadline date. So did consumer advocates and ERCOT itself. The project index now stands at 67 filings. The commission next considers the proposal at an open meeting before adopting a final rule.

items.title: TRAIGA in force as Business and Commerce Code Chapter 552, enforceable only by the Attorney General
items.summary: The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act took effect on January 1st, 2026 as Chapter 552 of the Business and Commerce Code. It bans developing or deploying an AI system with intent to unlawfully discriminate, to manipulate behavior, for social scoring or to produce certain illegal content. It also requires government agencies to tell people when they are interacting with an AI system. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and the statute creates no private right of action.

decider.name: Office of the Attorney General of Texas

key_dates.note: HB 149 signed by the Governor
Chapter 552 took effect

public_access.how: Individuals can't sue under this chapter. The route is a complaint to the Attorney General. The same chapter requires that office to create and maintain an online mechanism on its website through which a consumer may submit a complaint.

claims.text: The chapter was created by HB 149 and took effect January 1st, 2026.
claims.verbatim_quote: Added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1174 (H.B. 149), Sec. 4, eff. January 1, 2026.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Chapter 552, Artificial Intelligence Protection, source note to Sec. 552.001

claims.text: The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and there is no private right of action.
claims.verbatim_quote: (a) The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce this chapter, except to the extent provided by Section  552.106 . (b) This chapter does not provide a basis for, and is not subject to, a private right of action for a violation of this chapter or any other law.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.101, Enforcement Authority

claims.text: The statute sets tiered civil penalties by violation type.
claims.verbatim_quote: (1) for each violation the court determines to be curable or a breach of a statement submitted to the attorney general under Section  552.104 (b)(2), not less than $10,000 and not more than $12,000; (2) for each violation the court determines to be uncurable, not less than $80,000 and not more than $200,000; and (3) for a continued violation, not less than $2,000 and not more than $40,000 for each day the violation continues.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.105, Civil Penalty; Injunction

claims.text: The discrimination ban turns on intent, and disparate impact alone is not enough to show it.
claims.verbatim_quote: (b) A person may not develop or deploy an artificial intelligence system with the intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class in violation of state or federal law. (c) For purposes of this section, a disparate impact is not sufficient by itself to demonstrate an intent to discriminate.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.056, Unlawful Discrimination

claims.text: Government agencies must disclose AI interaction even when it would be obvious.
claims.verbatim_quote: (c) A person is required to make the disclosure under Subsection (b) regardless of whether it would be obvious to a reasonable consumer that the consumer is interacting with an artificial intelligence system.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.051, Disclosure to Consumers

claims.text: There is a rebuttable presumption that a person used reasonable care.
claims.verbatim_quote: (c) There is a rebuttable presumption that a person used reasonable care as required under this chapter.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.105, Civil Penalty; Injunction

claims.text: The chapter requires the Attorney General to run an online complaint mechanism.
claims.verbatim_quote: The attorney general shall create and maintain an online mechanism on the attorney general's Internet website through which a consumer may submit a complaint under this chapter to the attorney general.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.102, Information and Complaints

items.notes_for_editor: Sourced to the enacted statute rather than to the bill history, which is both the better primary source and an allowed one. Dollar figures appear only inside verbatim statutory quotes. Note the chapter title is Artificial Intelligence Protection, not the act's popular name.

items.title: Utilities Code limits how the PUCT may direct ERCOT, and bars verbal directives
items.summary: Texas law restricts the channels through which the Public Utility Commission may order ERCOT to act. A verbal directive is prohibited outright. An official action may be directed only by contested case, by rulemaking or by a written order or memorandum adopted on a majority vote. The ERCOT board selection committee picks ERCOT's directors and designates its chair. The governor does not.

key_dates.note: SB 2 (87R) added the board selection committee

public_access.how: A directive to ERCOT must run through a contested case, a rulemaking or a majority vote taken in a meeting. Each of those routes carries its own way in for the public. PUCT open meetings are listed on the agency calendar feed and are open to the public in Commissioners Hearing Room 7-100.

claims.text: The commission may not verbally direct ERCOT and may direct official action only three ways.
claims.verbatim_quote: (a) The commission may not use a verbal directive to direct an independent organization certified under Section 39.151 to take an official action. The commission may direct the organization to take an official action only through: (1) a contested case; (2) rulemaking; or (3) a memorandum or written order adopted by a majority vote.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1514, Commission Directives to Independent Organization

claims.text: The ERCOT board selection committee is three members, one each appointed by the governor, lieutenant governor and speaker.
claims.verbatim_quote: (a) The ERCOT board selection committee is composed of: (1) one member appointed by the governor; (2) one member appointed by the lieutenant governor; and (3) one member appointed by the speaker of the house of representatives.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1513, ERCOT Board Selection Committee

claims.text: That committee selects ERCOT's governing body and designates its chair and vice chair.
claims.verbatim_quote: (d) The committee shall select members eligible under Section 39.151 to serve on the governing body of an independent organization certified under that section for the ERCOT power region and shall designate the chair and vice chair of the governing body from those members.
claims.source_title: Texas Utilities Code Sec. 39.1513, ERCOT Board Selection Committee

items.notes_for_editor: This item exists to give readers the legal frame for the August 3rd audit directive. It states what the statute says and stops there. It does NOT assert that the governor's directive was improper: the section binds the commission's directives to ERCOT, and a governor's letter to both agencies is a different instrument. Any characterisation beyond the quoted text needs a lawyer and a named source.

items.title: Texas Government Code Chapter 2054 carries three conflicting Subchapter S's on AI, with duplicated section numbers
items.summary: Three separate acts of the 89th Legislature each added a Subchapter S to Government Code Chapter 2054, and two of them number their sections identically. Section 2054.702 exists twice with entirely different commands, as do Sections 2054.701 and 2054.703 through 2054.705. The codifier has flagged the conflict in the published code rather than resolved it. Which text governs a state agency's AI duties is unsettled on the face of the statute.

key_dates.note: Both conflicting AI subchapters took effect

public_access.how: A codification conflict is resolved either by the Legislature in a future non substantive revision bill or by a court. There is no comment window. A reader who cares can raise it with their own legislator or with the Texas Legislative Council, which prepares the revision bills.

claims.text: The published code carries an editorial note recording three separate Subchapter S enactments.
claims.verbatim_quote: Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.713, was added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1148 (S.B.  1964 ), Sec. 5. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.651 to 2054.654, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 951 (H.B.  5195 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.651 et seq., post. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.705, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1079 (H.B.  2818 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.701 et seq., post.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Chapter 2054, editorial note preceding Subchapter S

claims.text: One version of Section 2054.702 concerns generative AI technology.
claims.verbatim_quote: Sec. 2054.702. GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGY.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702, in the Subchapter S added by HB 2818

claims.text: The other version of Section 2054.702 requires a statewide AI code of ethics.
claims.verbatim_quote: Sec. 2054.702. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEM CODE OF ETHICS.  (a) The department by rule shall establish an artificial intelligence system code of ethics for use by state agencies and local governments that procure, develop, deploy, or use artificial intelligence systems.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702, in the Subchapter S added by SB 1964

claims.text: That code of ethics must align with a named federal framework.
claims.verbatim_quote: the artificial intelligence system code of ethics must include guidance for the deployment and use of artificial intelligence systems and heightened scrutiny artificial intelligence systems that aligns with the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702(b), in the Subchapter S added by SB 1964

claims.text: Local governments as well as state agencies must adopt the code of ethics.
claims.verbatim_quote: (c) State agencies and local governments shall adopt the code of ethics developed under this section.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.702(c), in the Subchapter S added by SB 1964

items.notes_for_editor: Found by reading the code, not reported anywhere we saw, and it is the strongest original finding in this seed set. The conflict is real and is visible in the state's own published text. One caution for the write up: duplicate subchapter designations are a routine artefact of a busy session and are usually cleaned up in the next non substantive revision bill, so the honest framing is that the code currently carries a conflict, not that anyone did something wrong. Worth checking whether the 89th Legislature's later called sessions already fixed it.

items.title: DIR must run an AI regulatory sandbox letting state agencies test systems outside normal rules
items.summary: The Department of Information Resources is required to establish a program letting eligible public entities contract with registered vendors to test AI systems before deployment. That testing is expressly without full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations. Vendors apply, and participants file quarterly reports. The department must report to the Legislature by November 30th of each even numbered year. That makes November 30th, 2026 the first reporting date.

key_dates.note: SB 1964 took effect
Department report to the Legislature due, per Sec. 2054.706(g)

public_access.how: The application process runs to vendors registered with DIR rather than to the general public. The statute provides no public comment step. The public visibility point is the report the department owes the Legislature by November 30th, 2026. A reader can ask DIR for the vendor application process and for any quarterly reports already filed.

claims.text: The sandbox is defined as testing without full regulatory compliance.
claims.verbatim_quote: "Program" means the program established by this section that is designed to allow temporary testing of an artificial intelligence system in a controlled, limited manner without requiring full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.706(a)(2), Artificial Intelligence System Sandbox Program

claims.text: The department must establish and administer the program.
claims.verbatim_quote: (b) The department shall establish and administer a program to support eligible entities in contracting with vendors to engage in research, development, training, testing, and other pre-deployment activities related to artificial intelligence systems
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.706(b)

claims.text: Vendor applications must include a public risk assessment and a mitigation plan.
claims.verbatim_quote: (2) a risk assessment of the system that addresses potential impacts on the public; and (3) a plan for mitigating any adverse consequences discovered during the system's testing phase.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.706(c)

claims.text: The department owes the Legislature a report on a fixed recurring date.
claims.verbatim_quote: (g) Not later than November 30 of each even-numbered year, the department shall produce an annual report and submit the report to the legislature summarizing:
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Sec. 2054.706(g)

claims.text: The sandbox was created by SB 1964, effective September 1st, 2025.
claims.verbatim_quote: Added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1148 (S.B.  1964 ), Sec. 5, eff. September 1, 2025.
claims.source_title: Texas Government Code Chapter 2054 Subchapter S, source note

items.notes_for_editor: CORRECTION TO A COMMON BELIEF, please keep it in the published item. The regulatory sandbox is widely attributed to TRAIGA. It is not in TRAIGA. It is Section 2054.706, added by SB 1964, and it took effect September 1st, 2025, four months before TRAIGA did. Whether DIR has actually stood the program up was NOT verified: no DIR page was fetched. That is the obvious follow up and the honest hook is the November 30th, 2026 report.

items.title: TRAIGA preempts city and county regulation of artificial intelligence
items.summary: Chapter 552 of the Business and Commerce Code supersedes and preempts any local ordinance, resolution, rule or regulation about the use of AI systems. Texas cities and counties that might otherwise write their own AI rules are displaced by the state statute. The preemption is written broadly and without a carve out on its face.

key_dates.note: Chapter 552 took effect, including the preemption section

public_access.how: The preemption is enacted law and takes no comment. Changing it takes the Legislature or a court. The Legislature next convenes in regular session in 2027. A resident whose city wants to act on AI can raise it with their legislator.

claims.text: The chapter preempts local regulation of AI use.
claims.verbatim_quote: Sec. 552.003. LOCAL PREEMPTION.  This chapter supersedes and preempts any ordinance, resolution, rule, or other regulation adopted by a political subdivision regarding the use of artificial intelligence systems.
claims.source_title: Texas Business and Commerce Code Sec. 552.003, Local Preemption

items.notes_for_editor: Kept as its own item because it is the provision most likely to collide with the local data center fights elsewhere in this docket. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION a fact checker must preserve: this preempts local rules about the USE OF AI SYSTEMS. A city zoning ordinance about data center buildings is land use regulation, not AI use regulation, so San Marcos's ban is NOT obviously preempted by this section. Do not let the two be conflated in the write up.

items.title: Comptroller's JETI current agreements list contains no data center project
items.summary: The Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act is the state's school district property tax incentive program. The Comptroller publishes the current executed agreements. Every project type on that list is manufacturing, power generation or extraction. No agreement on the published list is a data center.

public_access.how: The list is published for inspection and is not a proceeding. JETI applications are filed with and acted on by individual school districts. The participation point for a resident is their own district's board meeting when an application is before it.

items.title: Statute requires state agencies and local governments to post standardized notice of AI systems
items.summary: Every state agency and local government that deploys a public facing AI system must post a standardized notice on the related applications, websites and public computer systems. The same duty covers any system that is a controlling factor in a consequential decision. The Department of Information Resources is required to develop the notice form. That form must describe the system, its data sources and its privacy and ethics safeguards.

public_access.how: The notice is meant to appear wherever the system is used. A resident who meets a government AI system should be able to see one. claims.verbatim_quote: (a) Each state agency and local government deploying or using an artificial intelligence system that is public-facing or that is a controlling factor in a consequential decision shall include a standardized notice on all related applications, Internet websites, and public computer systems.

claims.text: DIR must develop the notice form and the statute fixes its minimum contents.

It asks voters about the police department's continued use of automated license plate reader cameras at fixed locations on public roadways. Mayor Long sponsored the item and asked for approval on first and final reading. items.summary: The Corpus Christi City Council passed a motion on July 21st, 2026 as agenda item 18, moved by Council Member Gilbert Hernandez and seconded by Council Member Carolyn Vaughn. The motion tells staff to initiate a Unified Development Code amendment defining data centers as a distinct principal land use. Staff are also to amend the zoning and permitted use tables to prohibit them in all districts. It also directs an extraterritorial jurisdiction and infrastructure protection policy. Under it a data center would fully fund its own infrastructure, provide verified water and wastewater planning and address electric and backup power impacts. It would need separate City Council approval before receiving city utility service or economic development incentives. A third part directs the statutory notice, hearing and findings work needed before the council could consider a temporary development moratorium. It tells the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to run a verification and audit of every data center moving through the interconnection process. items.title: Two Texas House committees take up data centers and AI in health care on August 19th and August 20th
items.summary: The House Committee on State Affairs meets on August 19th, 2026 on a charge covering data center development in Texas. The same charge names SB 6 and the large load batch study process the grid operator proposed, and its posted reading list carries the Governor's August 3rd directive letter. The House Committee on Public Health meets the following day on a charge covering artificial intelligence in health care. Both sit in the interim, before the 90th Legislature convenes.

key_dates.note: House Committee on State Affairs, data centers charge
House Committee on Public Health, artificial intelligence charge

public_access.how: Interim committee hearings are public and take invited and public testimony in Austin. The Legislative Reference Library posts the week's hearings with links to each agenda, and the agenda is where the room and the start time are published. A Texan who wants to be heard on a data center or on AI in a clinic has two dated chances this week.

claims.text: The State Affairs committee carries a data center charge in the interim.
claims.verbatim_quote: Charge: Data Centers: Study the development of data centers in Texas, including its importance to global competitiveness and national security.
claims.source_title: Legislative Reference Library of Texas, Interim Hearings, Week of August 17, 2026

claims.text: The same charge names SB 6 and the grid operator's batch study process for large loads.
claims.verbatim_quote: Study the implementation of SB 6 and the Large Load Batch Study Process proposed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, as it relates to data centers, and identify how grid-connected data center facilities and co-located resources can support grid resilience and reliability.
claims.source_title: Legislative Reference Library of Texas, State Affairs charge text

claims.text: The Public Health committee carries an artificial intelligence charge.
claims.verbatim_quote: Charge: Artificial Intelligence Use in Health Care: Study the use of artificial intelligence in the health care system to improve access, quality, and efficiency of care, while evaluating potential risks to patient safety, privacy, and access to care for Texans.
claims.source_title: Legislative Reference Library of Texas, Public Health charge text

claims.text: The reading list posted with the data center charge includes the Governor's August 3rd directive letter.
claims.verbatim_quote: (RE: Directing the PUC and ERCOT to take certain actions to shield customers from data infrastructure costs), Governor Greg Abbott, August 3, 2026
